summary.text: A reflecting telescope uses one curved mirror or a combination of them to reflect light and form an image.
Isaac Newton invented it in the 17th century as an alternative to the refractor, which then suffered from severe chromatic aberration.
The design allows very large diameter objectives, and almost all the major telescopes used in astronomy research are reflectors.

facts.label: Newton's telescope
facts.value: Built in 1668, considered the first reflecting telescope

facts.label: Leviathan of Parsonstown
facts.value: Largest 19th-century telescope, with a 1.8 m metal mirror

facts.label: Speculum metal
facts.value: Reflected only about two-thirds of the light

facts.label: Modern mirror coating
facts.value: A thin vacuum-deposited layer of aluminum

items.prompt: Reflectors had real theoretical advantages. Why did it still take over 100 years for them to become popular?

options.label: Nobody had yet thought of using a mirror
They were hard to build and their mirrors worked poorly
Lens makers would not share their glass
Mirrors could not form any real image

items.explain: The difficulty of construction and the poor performance of speculum metal mirrors delayed their popularity.

items.prompt: An observer in the early 1800s keeps re-polishing a metal telescope mirror that dulls quickly. What change helped by the middle of the century?

options.label: Making the mirror from a heavier metal
Swapping the mirror for a lens
Coating the mirror with a thin layer of paint
Using silvered-glass mirrors, which were cheaper and resisted tarnish

items.explain: Speculum metal tarnished easily and needed frequent re-polishing, so silvered glass became more popular for being cheaper and resistant to tarnish.

items.prompt: A researcher wants a telescope for wavelengths that glass partly absorbs. Which design suits better, and why?

options.label: A reflector, since the light bounces off a surface instead of passing through glass
A refractor, since glass focuses every wavelength well
A refractor, since its lens is the same everywhere
Neither, since all designs absorb the same amount

items.explain: Reflectors work in a wider spectrum of light because certain wavelengths are absorbed when passing through glass elements.

items.prompt: In most reflectors a secondary mirror or detector sits near the focal point, in front of the main mirror. What does that cost?

options.label: Colors fringing at the edge of every star
A much shorter focal length
Some lost light and some lost image contrast
A mirror that tarnishes more quickly

items.explain: The obstruction reduces the light collected and lowers contrast through diffraction effects, with spikes from the support structures.

items.prompt: A telescope maker compares a large lens with a large mirror of similar size. Which statement about flaws is right?

options.label: Both need flawless material through their whole volume
Neither needs any special care
A mirror needs flawless material throughout, but a lens needs only one good surface
A mirror needs just one perfectly polished surface, but a lens needs flawless material throughout

items.explain: In a lens the entire volume of material has to be free of imperfections, whereas in a mirror only one surface has to be perfectly polished.

items.prompt: Stars near the edge of a reflector's image smear into comet-like radial streaks, worse the farther from the center. Which flaw is this?

options.label: Distortion, which changes object shapes but not sharpness
Coma, which gets worse toward the edges
Field curvature, a curved best image plane
Astigmatism, which makes off-axis stars look elliptical

items.explain: Coma makes stars look like radial smudges that worsen toward the edges. The other flaws affect shape, focus across the field, or ellipticity instead.
